source.stem:
The table gives four energy sources and states whether the energy of the source is derived from the Sun.
Which row is correct?
source of energy derived from the Sun

options.text: water held behind a dam yes

mx.name: term_substitution
mx.teacher_note: Cooling water vapour forms clouds by evaporation.

mx.name: condition_omission
mx.teacher_note: Water vapour condenses into clouds simply by rising, even without cooling.

mx.name: relationship_reversal
mx.teacher_note: Condensation into clouds causes the rising water vapour to cool.

mx.name: scope_error
mx.teacher_note: Snow and hail are not part of the water cycle.

intelligence.enrichment: The Sun heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes so it evaporates as water vapour; plants release water vapour through transpiration; rising vapour cools and condenses to form clouds, and clouds bring precipitation. Solar heating produces water vapour, cooling aloft changes vapour into clouds, precipitation brings water down, and water returns through soil, rocks, plants, and water bodies in a continuous cycle. The learner correctly applies this rule: The Sun heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes so it evaporates as water vapour; plants release water vapour through transpiration; rising vapour cools and condenses to form clouds, and clouds bring precipitation. Rain appears from clouds without evaporation from water bodies or transpiration from plants.

spec.instruction: Write one new grades 7 Science question. Chapter: Heat transfer. The student must decide: Sequence the water cycle as Sun-driven evaporation and transpiration, rising and cooling of water vapour, condensation into clouds, precipitation, seepage or return flow, and return to water bodies. Use an Indian school or home setting and Indian names. Keep the source language register. Change the numbers, materials, or everyday situation. Do not copy the source stem. Recalculate the key. Do not print mix-up labels, hinge codes, node codes, or the word CANDIDATE.
